overview:
Myocardial ischemia occurs when blood flow to the heart is reduced, preventing the heart muscle from receiving enough oxygen. The reduced blood flow is usually the result of a partial or complete blockage of the heart's coronary arteries. Myocardial ischemia reduces the heart muscle's ability to pump blood. A sudden, severe blockage of one of the heart's arteries can lead to a heart attack. Myocardial ischemia might also cause serious abnormal heart rhythms.
+Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTEACS) encompasses two main entities: non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and unstable angina pectoris (UAP). The differentiation between these two conditions is usually retrospective, based on the presence or absence of raised cardiac enzymes at 8 to 12 hours after the onset of chest pain. Both produce the same spectrum of ECG changes and symptoms and are managed identically in the Emergency Department.
ecg_clues: dynamic ST segment changes compared with baseline
dynamic T wave changes compared with baseline
horizontal ST depression at the J-point
downsloping ST depression at the J-point
ST depression greater than or equal to 0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads
ST depression greater than or equal to 1 mm
ST depression greater than or equal to 2 mm in 3 leads
widespread ST depression in leads I II V4-6
ST elevation in aVR greater than 1 mm with widespread ST depression
T wave inversion at least 1 mm deep in 2 contiguous leads with dominant R waves
pseudonormalisation of previously inverted T waves
Wellens syndrome biphasic T waves in V2-4
Wellens syndrome deeply and symmetrically inverted T waves in V2-4
ecg_limitations: numerous conditions may simulate myocardial ischaemia such as left ventricular hypertrophy or digoxin effect
ST depression localized to a territory may represent reciprocal change from STEMI and requires evaluation for subtle ST elevation
T wave inversion is only significant when seen in leads with upright QRS complexes; it is a normal variant in leads III aVR and V1
differentiation between NSTEMI and unstable angina is usually retrospective and based on cardiac enzymes 8 to 12 hours after chest pain

common: shortness of breath when physically active
red_flags: chest pain that does not go away

causes: partial or complete blockage of a coronary artery
risk_factors: waist circumference greater than 35 inches in women or 40 inches in men

history_questions: What are your symptoms and when did they begin?
Are your symptoms occasional or continuous?
Does anything improve or worsen your symptoms?
Do you have a family history of heart disease high blood pressure or high cholesterol?
Do you smoke or did you smoke?
Do you have shortness of breath with activity?

goals: improve blood flow to the heart muscle
lifestyle: manage underlying health conditions such as diabetes high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol
eat whole grains fruits and vegetables

when_to_seek_help: chest pain that does not go away

followup_questions.chest_pain: Do you have chest pain or chest pressure?
followup_questions.angina: Do you have chest pressure or pain on the left side of your body?
followup_questions.neck_or_jaw_pain: Do you have neck or jaw pain?
followup_questions.shoulder_or_arm_pain: Do you have shoulder or arm pain?
followup_questions.shortness_of_breath: Do you get short of breath with physical activity?
followup_questions.fast_heartbeat: Have you noticed a fast heartbeat?
followup_questions.nausea_or_vomiting: Have you had nausea or vomiting?
followup_questions.sweating: Have you had sweating with symptoms?
followup_questions.silent_ischemia: Have you had episodes without symptoms but were told you had ischemia?
followup_questions.hypertension: Have you been diagnosed with high blood pressure?
followup_questions.high_cholesterol: Have you been told you have high cholesterol?
followup_questions.high_triglycerides: Have you been told you have high triglycerides?
followup_questions.tobacco_use: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
followup_questions.family_history_heart_disease: Do you have a family history of heart disease high blood pressure or high cholesterol?
followup_questions.exercise_level: How often do you exercise or do physical activity?

confidence_rules: dynamic ST segment and T wave changes strongly increase confidence for myocardial ischaemia
horizontal or downsloping ST depression greater than or equal to 0.5 mm at the J-point in 2 contiguous leads indicates myocardial ischaemia
ST depression greater than or equal to 1 mm is more specific
ST depression greater than or equal to 2 mm in 3 leads increases probability of NSTEMI
T wave inversion at least 1 mm deep in 2 contiguous leads with dominant R waves increases confidence
ST elevation in aVR greater than 1 mm with widespread ST depression suggests left main coronary artery occlusion
agent_reasoning_hints: NSTEACS includes NSTEMI and unstable angina and they share the same ECG changes and symptoms
Differentiation between NSTEMI and unstable angina is retrospective based on cardiac enzymes 8 to 12 hours after chest pain
Subendocardial ischemia produces widespread ST depression, often in leads I II V4-6
Regional ST depression should prompt scrutiny for subtle reciprocal ST elevation
T wave inversion is only significant in leads with dominant R waves and is normal in leads III aVR and V1
Wellens syndrome indicates critical LAD stenosis and a high risk of anterior MI within 2 to 3 weeks
U-wave inversion can be a specific sign of myocardial ischaemia
source_notes: NSTEACS includes NSTEMI and unstable angina and differentiation is retrospective based on cardiac enzymes 8 to 12 hours after chest pain
Dynamic ST segment and T wave changes strongly suggest myocardial ischaemia
Horizontal or downsloping ST depression of at least 0.5 mm at the J-point in 2 contiguous leads indicates myocardial ischaemia
ST depression of 1 mm is more specific and conveys worse prognosis
ST depression of 2 mm in 3 leads is associated with a high probability of NSTEMI and predicts significant mortality at 30 days
Widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR greater than 1 mm suggests left main coronary artery occlusion
T wave inversion is significant when at least 1 mm deep, present in 2 contiguous leads with dominant R waves, and dynamic
T wave inversion is normal in leads III aVR and V1
Wellens syndrome involves inverted or biphasic T waves in V2-4 and is highly specific for critical LAD stenosis
Wellens syndrome has Type A biphasic T waves and Type B deeply inverted T waves
U-wave inversion is an infrequently recognized but very specific sign of myocardial ischaemia
Myocardial ischemia reduces the heart muscle's ability to pump blood and can cause serious abnormal heart rhythms
Chest pain associated with myocardial ischemia can be triggered by physical exertion emotional stress cold temperatures cocaine use eating a heavy or large meal and sexual intercourse
